paragraphs: There was once a man who had fine houses in both town and country, a great deal of silver and gold tableware, embroidered furnishings, and coaches covered all over in gold. But unfortunately, this man had a blue beard, which made him so frighteningly ugly that all the women and girls ran away from him.

One of his neighbours, a lady of high social standing, had two daughters who were perfect beauties. He asked to marry one of them, leaving the mother to choose which daughter she would give him. Neither girl wanted him. They sent him back and forth between them, unable to bear the thought of marrying a man with a blue beard. They were also disgusted and repelled by the fact that he had already had several wives, and nobody ever knew what had become of them.

To win their affection, Blue Beard took them, their mother, three or four ladies they knew, and some other young people from the neighbourhood to one of his country houses. They stayed there for a whole week.

There was nothing but pleasure parties, hunting, fishing, dancing, laughter, and feasting. Nobody went to bed; they all spent the night teasing and joking with one another. Everything went so well that the younger daughter began to think the master of the house did not have such a very blue beard after all, and that he was an extremely polite gentleman.

As soon as they returned home, the marriage took place. About a month later, Blue Beard told his wife that he had to travel into the country for at least six weeks on very important business. He asked her to enjoy herself while he was away, to send for her friends and acquaintances, to take them into the country if she liked, and to feast and be merry wherever she was.

“Here,” he said, “are the keys to the two large storerooms where I keep my best furnishings. These are for my silver and gold tableware, which is not used every day. These open the strongboxes holding my money, both gold and silver; these open my jewel boxes; and this is the master key to all my rooms. But this little one here is the key to the small room at the end of the long gallery on the ground floor. Open everything. Go into every one of them except that little room, which I forbid you to enter. And understand my order clearly: if you do open it, there is nothing you may not expect from my justified anger and resentment.”
She promised to follow all his orders exactly. He embraced her, got into his coach, and set off on his journey.

The newly married lady’s neighbours and good friends did not wait to be invited. They were so impatient to see all the splendid furnishings in her house. They had not dared to come while her husband was there, because his blue beard frightened them. They ran through all the rooms, little chambers, and storerooms, each of which seemed finer and more richly furnished than the last.

Then they went upstairs into the two great rooms, which contained the best and richest furnishings. They could not admire enough the number and beauty of the tapestries, beds, couches, cabinets, stands, tables, and mirrors in which you could see yourself from head to foot. Some mirrors had glass frames, others silver ones, either plain or gilded: the finest and most magnificent ever seen.

They never stopped praising and envying their friend’s happiness. Meanwhile, she took no pleasure in looking at all these rich possessions, because she was so impatient to open the little room on the ground floor. Her curiosity pressed her so hard that she hurried down a small back staircase, without considering how rude it was to leave her guests. She went so fast that she almost broke her neck two or three times.

When she reached the door of the little room, she stopped for a while. She thought about her husband’s orders and the misery that might follow if she disobeyed. But the temptation was too strong to resist. She took the little key and opened the door, trembling. At first she could not see anything clearly, because the windows were shut. After a few moments, she began to make out a floor entirely covered in clotted blood. On it lay the bodies of several dead women, arranged along the walls. (These were all the wives Blue Beard had married and murdered, one after another.) She thought she would die of fright. The key she had pulled from the lock fell from her hand.

When she had recovered a little from the shock, she picked up the key, locked the door, and went upstairs to her bedroom to calm herself. But she was too frightened to do so. Noticing that the key to the little room was stained with blood, she tried two or three times to wipe it clean. The blood would not come off. She washed it in vain, even rubbing it with soap and sand, but the stain remained. The key was magical, and she could never get it completely clean. Whenever the blood disappeared from one side, it came back on the other.

Blue Beard returned from his journey that same evening. He said he had received letters on the road telling him that the business he had set out to deal with had been settled in his favour. His wife did everything she could to convince him that she was extremely glad he had returned so soon.
The next morning he asked for the keys. She gave them to him, but her hand trembled so much that he easily guessed what had happened.
“What!” he said. “Is the key to my little room not here with the others?”
“I must have left it upstairs on the table,” she said.
“Make sure you bring it to me at once,” said Blue Beard.
After going back and forth several times, she was forced to bring him the key. Blue Beard examined it very carefully, then said to his wife:
“How did this blood get onto the key?”
“I don’t know,” cried the poor woman, paler than death.

“You don’t know!” Blue Beard replied. “I know perfectly well. You were determined to go into that little room, weren’t you? Very well, madam. You shall go in and take your place among the ladies you saw there.”

She threw herself at her husband’s feet and begged his forgiveness, showing every sign of true repentance and promising never to disobey him again. She was so beautiful and so sorrowful that she could have melted a rock. But Blue Beard’s heart was harder than any rock!
“You must die, madam,” he said, “and at once.”
“Since I must die,” she answered, looking at him through eyes bathed in tears, “give me a little time to say my prayers.”
“I give you seven and a half minutes,” Blue Beard replied, “but not one moment more.”
When she was alone, she called out to her sister and said:
“Sister Anne”—for that was her name—“please go up to the top of the tower and see whether my brothers are coming. They promised to come today. If you see them, signal to them to hurry.”
Her sister Anne went up to the top of the tower, and the poor, distressed wife called out from time to time:
“Anne, sister Anne, do you see anyone coming?”
And sister Anne said:
“I see nothing but the sun making the dust shimmer, and the grass looking green.”
Meanwhile Blue Beard, holding a great sabre in his hand, shouted to his wife as loudly as he could:
“Come down at once, or I shall come up to you.”
“One moment longer, please,” his wife said. Then she called out very softly, “Anne, sister Anne, do you see anyone coming?”
And sister Anne answered:
“I see nothing but the sun making the dust shimmer, and the grass that is green.”
“Come down quickly,” Blue Beard cried, “or I will come up to you.”
“I’m coming,” his wife answered. Then she called, “Anne, sister Anne, don’t you see anyone coming?”
“I see a great cloud of dust coming this way,” sister Anne replied.
“Are they my brothers?”
“Sadly, no, my dear sister. I see a flock of sheep.”
“Will you come down?” Blue Beard shouted.
“One moment longer,” his wife said. Then she called out, “Anne, sister Anne, do you see no one coming?”
“I see two horsemen,” she said, “but they are still a long way off.”
“God be praised!” the poor wife answered joyfully. “They are my brothers. I will signal to them as well as I can to make them hurry.”
Then Blue Beard roared so loudly that he made the whole house shake. His distressed wife came downstairs and threw herself at his feet, weeping, with her hair hanging over her shoulders.

“This means nothing,” Blue Beard said. “You must die.” He took hold of her hair with one hand and raised his sword with the other, preparing to cut off her head. The poor lady turned towards him and looked at him with the eyes of someone about to die. She begged him to give her one little moment to collect herself.
“No, no,” he said. “Entrust yourself to God.” He was just about to strike…

At that very instant, there was such a loud knocking at the gate that Blue Beard stopped abruptly. The gate opened, and two horsemen immediately came in. Drawing their swords, they ran straight at Blue Beard. He recognised them as his wife’s brothers, one a dragoon and the other a musketeer, and immediately ran away to save himself. But the two brothers pursued him so closely that they caught him before he could reach the porch steps. They ran their swords through his body and left him dead. The poor wife was almost as lifeless as her husband and had no strength to get up and welcome her brothers.

Blue Beard had no heirs, so his wife inherited his entire estate. She used part of it to arrange her sister Anne’s marriage to a young gentleman who had loved her for a long time. She used another part to buy army commissions as captains for her brothers, and the rest for her own marriage to a very worthy gentleman, who made her forget the terrible time she had spent with Blue Beard.
